claims.text: A multiscale machine-learning framework can integrate first-principles phonon and electron scattering data, oxygen-defect configurations, and conductivity measurements.
The proposed framework can decouple lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen over 200–1200 K.
The proposed framework will reduce predictive error from 20–30% to below 10%.
The target material is polycrystalline, equimolar HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The target alloy exhibits realistic atomic-scale disorder.
The model will be trained using ab initio scattering rates and experimental conductivity data from low- and high-temperature regimes.
Lattice distortions produce phonon scattering in the target alloy.
Oxygen interstitials act as electron-scattering defect sites in the target alloy.
Phonon scattering from lattice distortion and electron scattering from oxygen defects govern thermal transport in the alloy.
Learning computed scattering parameters together with measured conductivity signals allows the model to distinguish phonon and electronic conductivity.
Independent lattice and electronic conductivity predictions will agree with separately determined experimental values to within 10% across 200–1200 K.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are comparable below 200 K in HfNbTaTiZr.
Existing relevant methods use defect-free models, Debye-temperature approximations, or independent treatments of phonon and electronic transport.
Existing methods generally have 20–30% predictive error.
Existing methods do not account for defect-induced scattering.
The model is expected to remain robust from 200 to 1200 K.
Below 200 K, additional phonon-electron coupling may reduce predictive reliability.
Above 1200 K, phase changes and unmodeled scattering mechanisms may reduce predictive reliability.
Combined laser-flash and thermoelectric/electrical characterization can provide experimentally separate estimates of lattice and electronic conductivity.
Electronic conductivity can be estimated using the Wiedemann–Franz law and measured electrical conductivity, with lattice conductivity derived from the remaining total conductivity.

contradictions.description: The stated applicability range begins at 200 K and the boundary warns that predictions below 200 K may be unreliable, yet the predicted outcome requires the model to reproduce comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K.
The experiment measures only 200–1200 K, but the falsification rule requires testing whether the model captures behavior below 200 K.

The hypothesis emphasizes non-conflated, independent lattice and electronic predictions, while the proposed experimental separation estimates electronic conductivity through the Wiedemann–Franz law and derives lattice conductivity from total conductivity; these are model-dependent derived quantities rather than fully independent direct measurements.
